common_name: Donation Camellia (Classic Pink Williamsii Hybrid Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Donation is one of the hardiest and most floriferous camellia hybrids and, unlike many camellias, sheds its own spent blooms cleanly instead of holding on to browned flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to keep the shallow roots cool and evenly moist through summer. Donation is a Camellia x williamsii hybrid, a cross between C. japonica and the more cold- and sun-tolerant C. saluenensis, and it combines the best traits of both parents: a vigorous, upright, densely branched habit smothered in late winter to early spring with large, semi-double, clear orchid-pink flowers. It is widely regarded as one of the finest garden camellias ever raised, prized not only for its heavy, reliable bloom but also for cleanly dropping its faded flowers on its own, sparing gardeners the tedious deadheading that camellias with browning, persistent blooms require. It tolerates more sun and cooler conditions than many Camellia japonica cultivars, though afternoon shade still helps prevent leaf scorch in hot Gulf South summers, and it needs little pruning beyond light shaping right after bloom.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Amur daylily is among the most cold-hardy species in the genus and blooms notably early, often the first daylily to flower in the garden each year.

directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade, and water well through the first season to establish. Native to the Russian Far East, Korea, Japan, and northern China, Hemerocallis middendorffii is a wild species daylily bearing clusters of fragrant, rich orange-yellow flowers held tightly atop relatively short, sturdy scapes well ahead of most modern daylily cultivars, typically opening in late spring to early summer. Its compact, clumping habit, cold hardiness, and early bloom time make it a useful species for extending the daylily season and for breeding programs, and it has been an important parent in the development of many early-flowering hybrid daylilies. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering, and expect the plant to seed itself modestly in favorable conditions since it is a true species rather than a sterile hybrid.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; grass-leaf daylily stays notably compact and narrow-leaved compared with modern hybrids, making it useful for the front of a border or a smaller garden.

directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, and keep evenly watered while the fans establish. Native across Siberia, northern China, Korea, and Japan, Hemerocallis minor is a dwarf wild species with fine, narrow, grass-like foliage and lightly fragrant, clear lemon-yellow flowers on slender scapes in early summer, considerably smaller in every dimension than modern hybrid daylilies. Its diminutive scale, cold hardiness, and long history in cultivation have made it a valued parent species in daylily breeding, particularly for miniature and dwarf hybrid lines. The tidy, non-spreading clumps rarely need division more than once every four or five years, and the fine-textured foliage remains attractive even when the plant isn't in bloom, unlike the coarser foliage of many large-flowered hybrids.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, giving the very tall flower scapes a sheltered spot at the back of a border; Tall Night-Blooming Daylily opens its flowers in late afternoon and evening rather than in the morning like most daylilies.

directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, siting toward the back of a bed where its exceptionally tall scapes won't shade shorter neighbors. Native to China, Hemerocallis altissima is one of the tallest species in the genus, sending up slender flower stalks well over 5 feet topped with clusters of pale yellow, sweetly fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers that open in late afternoon and stay open through the night, closing again by the following midday, an unusual habit among daylilies that mostly bloom for a single day. This late-summer bloom time and strongly evening-fragrant character make it a valuable addition to a moon garden or evening seating area where its perfume can be enjoyed after dusk. Established clumps are long-lived and rarely need division more than once every five years or so.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Dumortier's daylily is one of the earliest daylilies to bloom each year, often flowering weeks ahead of most hybrid cultivars.

directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade. Native to Japan, Korea, and northeastern China, Hemerocallis dumortieri is a low, early-blooming wild species bearing golden-orange flowers with buds distinctively tinged brownish-purple on the exterior before they open, held on relatively short, sturdy scapes just above the compact clump of foliage. Its notably early bloom time, well ahead of most daylily cultivars, and its cold hardiness make it useful both as a species collector's plant and as breeding stock for extending the daylily season into the earliest weeks of the growing year. The tidy, compact clumps are slow to spread and rarely require division more than once every several years to stay vigorous.

common_name: Cardinal de Richelieu Rose (Deep Purple-Violet Gallica Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Cardinal de Richelieu is a classic 19th-century Gallica rose, blooming once in a single heavy spring flush like other old Gallicas.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Cardinal de Richelieu tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough 19th-century Gallica. Introduced in France in the 1840s, it bears richly fragrant, fully double flowers that open deep magenta-crimson and age to a striking dark purple-violet, among the darkest colors found in old garden roses, set against dense, relatively thornless, arching canes and matte green foliage. Like other Gallicas it blooms just once, in a spectacular, heavily perfumed flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season, so it suits a mixed shrub border or dedicated old-rose garden better than a spot where repeat bloom is expected. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering rather than the intensive spray programs modern roses often require.

common_name: Belle Story Rose (Soft Pink Fragrant English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; like other David Austin English roses, Belle Story repeats reliably through the season with good deadheading and regular feeding.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and feed and water consistently through the growing season to sustain repeat flushes of bloom. Belle Story is a David Austin English shrub rose bearing large, cupped, semi-double flowers in soft blush pink surrounding a boss of prominent golden stamens, giving each bloom an open, almost peony-like or wild-rose look, backed by a strong, sweet myrrh-and-honey fragrance typical of many English roses. Its bushy, well-branched growth habit and repeat-flowering nature from late spring through fall make it a versatile choice for a mixed border or dedicated rose bed, combining the romantic form and scent of old garden roses with the modern trait of reblooming rather than flowering just once. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to encourage the next flush, and watch for blackspot in humid Gulf South summers, providing good air circulation and a preventive fungicide program if the disease has been a problem in the garden.
